forward-stroke.text: Sit tall and relax your grip — a loose top hand paddles further.
Wind up your torso; power comes from rotation, not the arms.
Plant the blade up near your feet, then pull back to your hip.
Slice the blade out cleanly at the hip — don't drag it past.
Fix your eyes on a point ahead; a steady gaze steadies your line.
Keep a light, even cadence on both sides.

reverse-stroke.text: Look over one shoulder before you move, and keep looking that way.
Use the back of the blade — there is no need to turn the paddle over.
Start each stroke at your hip and push it away towards the stern.
Unwind your torso with the blade; the arms only hold the shape.
Correct with a short reverse sweep, not with a forward stroke.
In wind the stern hunts — correct early and small, before it swings.

stopping.text: Sit up — braking starts from posture, not the arms.
Plant the blade fully in the water before you resist.
Use short, firm back-strokes on alternating sides.
Keep the boat flat; leaning back loosens your control.
Practise stopping from reverse too, not just from forward.

sweep.text: Reach the blade well forward, then draw a wide arc out to the stern.
Bury the whole blade — a skimming blade turns nothing.
Edge the kayak away from the turn to free up the ends.
Look where you want to go; the boat follows your eyes.
Turn from the torso — the arms only carry the paddle round.
Hold the edge through the whole arc, not just the start of it.

spinning.text: Link a forward sweep on one side to a reverse sweep on the other.
Keep both arcs wide, so the boat spins instead of travelling.
Change the edge as you change the stroke.
Spot round the horizon — watching your blade stalls the spin.
Count your strokes, then try the full circle in fewer.

turning-on-the-move.text: Set the turn up early — start it before you reach the obstacle.
Keep some speed; a moving hull turns, a stopped one does not.
Edge away from the turn and hold that edge through the arc.
Blend a sweep into your forward strokes — do not stop paddling.
Look through the turn to your exit, not at what you are avoiding.
Upwind and downwind turns need different edge — practise both.

draw.text: Stack your hands: top hand high, shaft as near vertical as you can.
Plant the blade out beside your hip, level with your body.
Pull the boat to the blade, not the blade to the boat.
Stop short of the hull, then slice the blade back out to start again.
If the bow leads, move the blade back; if the stern leads, move it forward.

stern-rudder.text: Rotate and lay the blade alongside the stern, close to the hull.
Carry some speed — a rudder needs water flowing past the blade.
Open the blade face away from the hull to turn towards the paddle.
Push the blade out from the stern to turn away from the paddle.
Hold the shaft with your torso, not your arms; stay wound up.
In following seas, rudder on the wave face and edge to hold your line.

edge-control.text: Edge with your knees and hips; keep your head over the boat.
Edge, do not lean — the body stays upright while the hull tilts.
Hold one edge steady, without a wobble, on each side.
Pick the edge before the stroke, not after it.
Hold the edge for the whole maneuver, then come flat on purpose.
Find how far you can go before the deck catches — then work just inside it.

low-brace-recovery.text: Knuckles down: the back of the blade slaps flat on the water.
Keep your elbows high and above the shaft, never behind you.
Push off the water and recover fast — do not rest your weight on it.
Snap the boat up with your knee and hip; the blade only buys time.
Your head comes up last, every time.
Practise going properly off balance, so the brace becomes a reflex.

low-brace-turn.text: Build speed first — the turn feeds on your momentum.
Open with a strong forward sweep to start the boat round.
Edge into the turn and hold it; the brace keeps you there.
Keep the blade flat and skimming just behind your hip.
Look through the turn and stay wound up until the boat comes round.
Vary the edge to widen or tighten the arc.

wet-exit.text: Stay calm — you have more time underwater than it feels.
Tuck forward onto the front deck before you release.
Find the grab loop and pull it forward with a committed sweep.
Push the cockpit rim off your thighs, then somersault out.
Keep one hand on the boat and one on the paddle after you exit.
